slide.heading: Blood Pressure
slide.subheading: MAP = CO × TPR, and how the body defends it

lines.text: Back in Hall B. Last week the heart was a pump; today, the pressure it creates, and how tightly your body holds it steady.
Mean arterial pressure is cardiac output times total peripheral resistance. Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume; resistance is set mostly by the arterioles.
Every drug we use for blood pressure changes one of these boxes.

slide.heading: Mean arterial pressure
bullets: MAP = CO × TPR
MAP ≈ diastolic + ⅓ (systolic − diastolic)
Diastole is longer, so MAP sits nearer diastolic
Organs are perfused by the MAP

lines.text: Your patients' organs are perfused by the mean pressure, not the systolic.
Because the heart spends longer in diastole, the mean sits closer to the diastolic: roughly diastolic plus a third of the pulse pressure.

slide.heading: The baroreceptor reflex
bullets: Stretch receptors in the carotid sinus (IX) and aortic arch (X)
Signal to the nucleus tractus solitarius
BP up: more vagal, less sympathetic output
Standing up: BP falls, HR and resistance rise
Fast, but resets in chronic hypertension

nodes.label: Carotid sinus and aortic arch fire more

lines.text: The fastest defense is a reflex. Stretch receptors in the carotid sinus, carried by the glossopharyngeal nerve, and in the aortic arch, by the vagus, report the pressure beat by beat to the brainstem.
Pressure up: they fire more, the brainstem turns up vagal tone and turns down sympathetic output, and the heart slows and vessels relax.
Stand up quickly and the reverse happens. Blood pools in your legs, pressure dips, and within seconds your heart speeds up and your arterioles squeeze.
When the reflex is sluggish, from age, drugs or autonomic disease, standing makes people dizzy: orthostatic hypotension.

slide.heading: Renin, angiotensin, aldosterone
bullets: Low renal perfusion: renin from juxtaglomerular cells
Angiotensinogen → angiotensin I → (ACE) → angiotensin II
Ang II: vasoconstriction, aldosterone, thirst, ADH
Aldosterone: Na⁺ and water kept, K⁺ lost
ACE also breaks down bradykinin

lines.text: The slower defense is hormonal. When the kidney senses low perfusion, its juxtaglomerular cells release renin.
Renin cuts angiotensinogen to angiotensin one; angiotensin-converting enzyme, mostly in the lungs, makes angiotensin two.
Angiotensin two constricts arterioles, releases aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone, and makes you thirsty. Aldosterone holds sodium and water and lets potassium go.
One more job for ACE: it breaks down bradykinin. Block ACE and bradykinin builds up, and you'll see why that matters in a minute.

slide.heading: Hypertension
bullets: Normal: < 120 and < 80
Elevated: 120–129 and < 80
Stage 2: ≥ 140 or ≥ 90
Confirm with repeated, out-of-office readings

lines.text: Hypertension is the commonest thing you'll treat, and it's silent until it causes a stroke, a heart attack, heart failure or kidney disease.

The categories in the U.S. guideline: normal below one-twenty over eighty; elevated one-twenty to one-twenty-nine; stage one, one-thirty to one-thirty-nine or eighty to eighty-nine; stage two, one-forty or ninety and above.
Never diagnose from one reading. Measure properly, repeat it, and confirm with home or ambulatory readings.

slide.heading: The drugs, and their catches
bullets: Thiazides: low K⁺ and Na⁺, high Ca²⁺ and urate
ACE inhibitors: cough, angioedema, high K⁺
ARBs: block the Ang II receptor; no bradykinin cough
ACE inhibitors and ARBs: not in pregnancy
Amlodipine (dihydropyridine CCB): ankle swelling

lines.text: First-line drugs: a thiazide diuretic, an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker, or a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker like amlodipine.
Thiazides can lower potassium and sodium and raise calcium and uric acid, which can bring on gout.
ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin, which causes a dry cough in some patients and, rarely, angioedema. They can also raise potassium.
Angiotensin receptor blockers act one step later, don't touch bradykinin, and rarely cause the cough.
Both are harmful to the fetal kidney, so neither is used in pregnancy.

slide.heading: Summary
bullets: MAP = CO × TPR
Baroreflex: seconds; RAAS: hours to days
Stage 1 starts at 130/80
ACEi cough → switch to an ARB

lines.text: The reflex defends pressure in seconds; the kidney, over days. Your drugs lean on both.
